title: Visitor and Room
premise: Pest controller Oscar Thackeray is called to a house where the infestation leaves fingerprints, and his refusal to believe becomes a liability when his grandmother's photographs begin showing an extra chair — with something sitting in it. The house was never haunted; it was leased, generations ago, to an entity that renews its tenancy by getting a living resident to sign papers of invitation. As the entity closes in on grandma Ruth, Oscar must choose between protecting her with comforting lies or telling her the truth about what their family invited in — because only a willing, informed refusal before sunrise can void the lease. He tells the truth; she refuses to sign; the last resident's claim collapses at dawn, but the house keeps one chair as a reminder that leases can be rewritten.
about_author: Ansel Crane is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade crawling through other people's basements and swears half of them were occupied. They write horror about property, inheritance, and the fine print nobody reads.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Oscar, third-generation pest controller, takes a routine job at a house where the 'infestation' left greasy fingerprints on the inside of sealed walls. His skeptical POV establishes his creed: everything has an explanation. Emotional beat: cocky competence masking a childhood fear of his grandmother's back room.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Oscar inspects the Crawshaw house and finds handprints that match no animal, trailing toward a locked cellar door the owner swears doesn't exist on any blueprint. POV: Oscar. Beat: first crack in his disbelief — the prints are fresh, and he was alone in the house.

chapters.title: Grandma's Album
chapters.summary: Visiting Ruth for Sunday dinner, Oscar notices every family photograph now contains an extra wooden chair against the wall — including photos taken decades ago. POV: Oscar. Beat: unease curdling into dread as Ruth cheerfully insists the chair has always been there.

chapters.title: The Tenant Above
chapters.summary: Ruth hears footsteps overhead in her single-story bungalow, polite and patient, like someone pacing a waiting room. POV: Ruth. Beat: loneliness — she almost welcomes the company, which frightens her more than the sounds.

chapters.title: Paperwork
chapters.summary: Oscar returns to the Crawshaw house and finds the cellar open: inside, a desk, a ledger of signatures spanning 140 years, and a blank contract titled 'Renewal of Residency.' POV: Oscar. Beat: vertigo — his own grandfather's name is in the ledger.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Oscar researches the family name and learns great-great-grandfather signed away 'right of dwelling' during the Depression to save the farm. POV: Oscar. Beat: shame and anger — the debt was inherited, never disclosed.

chapters.title: Chair Check
chapters.summary: Ruth wakes to find the extra chair moved from the photographs' background to the foreground, facing her bed. She covers it with a sheet; by morning the sheet is folded neatly on the seat. POV: Ruth. Beat: defiance hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Colleagues
chapters.summary: Oscar consults Marisol, a retired exterminator who handled 'the odd jobs,' and she confirms the pattern: houses under lease, families as guarantors, sunrise deadlines. POV: Oscar. Beat: reluctant found-family alliance; Marisol warns him truth-telling is the only legal defense.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: Ruth's health declines — doctors find nothing, but she's fading like a tenant being eased out. Oscar lies that it's nothing, protecting her. POV: Oscar. Beat: guilt; loyalty weaponized into concealment.

chapters.title: The Landlord Visits
chapters.summary: A courteous man in an old-fashioned suit appears at Ruth's door, calling himself the property manager, offering to 'simplify the paperwork.' POV: Ruth. Beat: charm laced with menace; she nearly signs out of politeness.

chapters.title: Marisol's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marisol shows Oscar records of families who told the truth too late — and one household that refused together and survived. The common factor: everyone present had to know and refuse. POV: Oscar. Beat: hope with a terrible condition attached.

chapters.title: Broken Trust
chapters.summary: Oscar finds Ruth signing preliminary documents in her sleepwalking state; he tears them up and confesses everything — the lease, the entity, his silence. POV: alternating. Beat: rage, then grief, then the fragile start of real partnership.

chapters.title: Preparations
chapters.summary: The trio fortifies the bungalow: salt lines as symbolic boundary, the original 1887 contract retrieved from county archives, witnesses arranged. POV: Oscar. Beat: purpose replacing panic; found family assembling its defenses.

chapters.title: Power Corrupts
chapters.summary: The property manager offers Oscar a deal: transfer the lease solely to himself, spare Ruth entirely, gain the house free and clear. POV: Oscar. Beat: temptation — power over the situation offered at the price of everyone else.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: Sunset. The house changes: hallways lengthen, the chair appears in every room, and the manager begins reading the contract aloud clause by clause. POV: Ruth. Beat: terror transmuted into stubborn attention — she listens to every word.

chapters.title: Clause Seventeen
chapters.summary: Midnight. The manager reveals the trap: uninformed residents count as consenting by default. Oscar's earlier lies nearly doom them all. POV: Oscar. Beat: self-loathing confronted; he owns every deception aloud.

chapters.title: Marisol Holds the Door
chapters.summary: The entity tests the boundaries through the Crawshaw house simultaneously; Marisol, guarding the archive copy, fends off the manager's duplicates. POV: Marisol. Beat: sacrifice-tinged courage; she buys the others time at personal cost.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Before dawn, Ruth stands before the chair and formally, knowingly, refuses renewal — speaking the truth of what her father-in-law invited in and rejecting the debt. POV: Ruth. Beat: triumph of clarity over fear; the climax.

chapters.title: Signatures Void
chapters.summary: The contract burns from the oldest signature down; the manager unravels mid-protest, and the chair collapses into ordinary wood. Sunrise floods the rooms. POV: Oscar. Beat: exhausted relief, disbelief finally allowed to rest.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Days later: Ruth recovers strength, Marisol heals, and the Crawshaw family quietly moves out of their freed house. POV: Oscar. Beat: tenderness; the found family solidifies around shared truth.

chapters.title: One Chair Remaining
chapters.summary: Oscar visits Ruth and finds one photograph still holds the chair — empty now, but present. Marisol confirms: leases end; landlords remember. POV: Oscar. Beat: sober vigilance, acceptance that some doors stay unlocked.

chapters.title: New Tenancy
chapters.summary: Epilogue: Oscar opens a small practice specializing in 'difficult properties,' training Ruth's neighbor's kid as an apprentice. The final image: him checking a new client's photographs — and finding nothing. Yet. POV: Oscar. Beat: earned peace shadowed by readiness; the watch continues.
